questions.question: What does it mean to sample from a centered discrete Gaussian over Z with parameter σ?
options: Choose an integer x with probability proportional to exp(-x^2/(2σ^2))
Choose a real x from N(0, σ^2) and keep it as a real number
Choose an integer uniformly from [-σ, σ]
Choose the shortest non-zero lattice vector
questions.explanation: A discrete Gaussian over integers assigns mass to each integer x proportional to exp(-x^2/(2σ^2)) (then normalizes).

questions.question: Why is a deterministic RNG useful when writing test vectors for a sampler?
options: It makes the same seed produce the same sample sequence across runs
It makes sampling constant-time by construction
It increases the variance of the sampled noise automatically
It removes the need to normalize probabilities
questions.explanation: Test vectors need reproducible outputs; a deterministic RNG provides stable sequences for a fixed seed and implementation.

questions.question: In a CDF-table sampler scaled to 2^64 buckets, what must the last CDF endpoint equal?
options: σ
The tail parameter t
questions.explanation: If you scale probabilities into 2^64 buckets, the cumulative sum must end at exactly 2^64.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the tail cut (truncation) parameter t in a discrete Gaussian sampler?
options: Make the infinite support finite by restricting to a window [c-t, c+t]
Ensure the sampled integers are always non-negative
Guarantee the distribution is exactly continuous Gaussian
Guarantee the sampler is constant-time
questions.explanation: Discrete Gaussians have infinite support; truncation makes a finite table at the cost of a small statistical error.

questions.question: If you increase σ (keeping the same center), what happens to the discrete Gaussian distribution over integers?
options: It spreads out and assigns more mass to larger |x| values
It concentrates more tightly at x = 0
It becomes uniform over the truncated window
It becomes supported only on even integers
questions.explanation: Larger σ increases the standard deviation, so larger-magnitude integers become more likely.

questions.question: Attack intuition: why is predictable randomness in a noise sampler dangerous for LWE-like constructions?
options: If an attacker can predict the noise, they can remove it and recover the underlying linear structure
It forces the lattice determinant to be 0, making the system singular
It makes Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization undefined
It makes the sampler output only zeros
questions.explanation: Noise is what hides the secret; predictable noise can let an attacker reconstruct clean equations and recover secrets.

questions.question: Attack intuition: what can go wrong if you truncate too aggressively (t too small) or bias the sampler?
options: The distribution can be distinguishable and effectively less noisy, which can weaken security
The sampled values become exactly uniform, which strengthens security
The distribution becomes independent of σ, which strengthens security
Nothing changes as long as σ is positive
questions.explanation: Heavy truncation or bias changes the intended distribution and can reduce effective noise, enabling distinguishers or easier lattice attacks.

questions.question: Why normalize probabilities into exact integer bucket counts (e.g. summing to 2^64) instead of relying on floating-point thresholds?
options: It makes the table deterministic and avoids cumulative rounding drift
It guarantees the sampler is cryptographically secure in Python
It guarantees the distribution has infinite support
It guarantees the distribution is perfectly continuous
questions.explanation: Using exact integer bucket totals gives stable, reproducible behavior and avoids floating-point edge cases in comparisons.
